# Top 20 AI Agent Pen-Testing Tools for 2026: The Ultimate Guide

--

Listen

Share

Traditionally, we have spent a lot of effort to automate a penetration test, mostly by automating individual tools. For example, Nuclei ran templates, ZAP crawled and scanned, Metasploit executed modules, and Burp Suite organized HTTP traffic and gave a human tester an excellent place to investigate it.

However, in 2026, AI agent can now sit above them, choose the next action, interpret and summarize the result, revise its hypothesis, and continue, just like professional human ethical hackers.

As a consequence, a lot of agent-native solutions and tools have poped up this year. Some try to automate and connect the existing softwares like Burp or ZAP with general-purpose agents, while others provides the agent-native solutions that are mostly headless CLI tools.

This article maps that landscape as it stands in September 2026. Note that this blog is not a ranking or recommendation, solely aiming to explain what each category is for, where representative tools fit, and what still remains unsolved.

## Category — 1: Automated pentesting

There are many services that try to provide the end-to-end process of pentesting as automated services. It typically includes defining a target and scope, lettting the system test it, and receiving validated findings, attack paths, or counter-examples.

### 1. XBOW

XBOW is a AI-native offsec platform that emulates hacker behaviors to find, chain, and validate critical vulnerabilities in software. XBOW has startted a lot of attentino after it achieved the top of HackerOne’s US leaderboard in 20205. It runs without a human supervision, and returns vulnerabilities with concrete evidences.

### 2. Horizon3.ai NodeZero

NodeZero focuses on autonomous pentesting across a broader situations, such as internal and external infrastructure, Active Directory, cloud, Kubernetes, and web applications. It tries to identify realistic attack paths that show how an attacker could exploit target environment and reach valuable assets, rather than just returring isolated lists of potential bugs.

### 3. Pentera

Pentera , one of the most popular automated seucirty tools, has been also shifting to AI-driven approach. Like NodeZero, it covers internal/external, cloud, identity, and application exposure.

### 4. Hadrian Nova

Hadrian combines external attack-surface discovery with continuous validation. It’s agentic pentesting feature lets AI agents analyze exposed assets, exuecute tests, and explore potential attack path.

### 5. Escape

Escape tests APIs, including GraphQL, and discovers endpoints without needing a schema uploaded first. It runs inside the software-delivery lifecycle

### 6. Aikido

Aikido Security also incorporates autonomous pentesting into a broader developer security platform. It positiones itself as all-in-one application security platform, and provides AI-driven pentesting, secrets and malware detection, and automatic bug fix.

### 7. Terra

Terra Security takes an explicitly human-supervised position within the commercial segment. Its agents run continuous, business-context-aware tests across web apps, APIs, mobile, internal applications, networks, and cloud.

## 2. Open-source autonomous agents

Open-source community on agentic security has been also evolving significantly.

### 8. Strix

Strix is an open-source application-security agent that fully automates the pentesting and bug fix worlflows. It dynamically runs code, tests applications, and attempts to validate findings with working proofs of concept. It can be also integrated with multiple agents, CLI and CI/CD workflows.

### 9. Shannon

Shannon is also an autonomous pentester for web applications and APIs. It combines source-code analysis with live exploitation, using the code to identify candidate attack paths and the running target to prove whether they are real.

### 10. PentAGI

PentAGI is a self-hosted multi-agent system for complex penetration-testing tasks. It gives agents access to security tooling and web search, separates roles, stores operational context, and provides an interface for supervising runs.

### 11. PentestGPT

PentestGPT first begans as an LLM-assisted penetration-testing workflow and has evolved toward a more agentic framework capable of planning and executing security and CTF tasks.

### 12. Nebula

Nebula deliberately takes a more human-led position. It combines a terminal, browser, editor, files, notes, findings, reports, and AI assistance in one engagement workspace. The operator defines scope and decides what runs.

### 13. CAI

CAI is an open-source framework for building your own security agents rather than a finished product. It provides agents, tools, handoffs, multi-agent patterns, and optional human-in-the-loop supervision, and it connects to the tooling a team already runs, such as Nmap or Burp.

> Note that CAI has been archived, though it’s source code is still available.

## 3. General-purpose agents connected to security tools

A second open-source movement starts with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or another general-purpose agent and gives it security capabilities. Model Context Protocol, or MCP, has become a common integration layer.

### 14. HexStrike AI

HexStrike AI is an MCP server that exposes a large collection of offensive-security tools to AI agents. Instead of building a proprietary reasoning system, it lets the user bring an agent and equips that agent to invoke scanners, recon tools, web-testing utilities, and exploitation frameworks.

### 15. Burp Suite’s MCP server and Burp AT

PortSwigger provides an official Burp Suite MCP Server extension , allowing AI clients to analyze traffic and interact with Burp programmatically. PortSwigger has also introduced Burp AT , an agentic capability inside Burp Suite Professional. It takes a human-led approach: the agent receives Burp’s project context and specialist tools, while the tester retains control of scope, tasks, and conclusions.

### 16. Caido

Caido is following a similar path with an AI skill and MCP-backed access to proxy traffic and testing operations. A general-purpose agent can inspect requests, send modified versions to replay, examine automation results, and work within the proxy context.

### 17. AutoPentest

AutoPentest packages web-testing workflows behind MCP, drawing on the OWASP Web Security Testing Guide and PortSwigger’s educational material. Many smaller projects expose Nmap, Nuclei, SQLMap, Metasploit, or custom recon pipelines in the same way.

## 4. Agent-native execution primitives

There are also many tools designed to give an agent a better way to observe or act.

### 18. h5i

h5i is an open-source, security-oriented headless browser for AI-driven red-teaming. It combines automated browsing with direct access to its own HTTP traffic. An agent can browse an application, capture requests, edit and replay them, compare responses, and run bounded recon through one command-line interface. It also provides several tiers of sandboxes to make the workflow safer.

### 19. Nuclei

Nuclei remains one of the most useful deterministic engines beneath an agent. Its YAML templates provide fast, reproducible checks across applications, infrastructure, and cloud services. An agent can use Nuclei for broad coverage, interpret the results, select follow-up tests, or generate a regression template after confirming a new issue.

### 20. OWASP ZAP

OWASP ZAP remains relevant because it provides a mature proxy, scanner, API, daemon mode, and YAML-based Automation Framework. Those are exactly the kinds of stable, inspectable capabilities an agent can orchestrate.

## 5. What is still unsolved

Triage came back. Autonomous validation was supposed to remove the false-positive problem. In practice a platform that produces hundreds of findings still hands the sorting work to a team that was already behind on alerts, and validation quality varies enough that the sorting cannot be skipped.

Chaining and business logic still favor humans. In the December 2025 ARTEMIS study on a live 8,000-host network, the best autonomous agent beat 9 of 10 OSCP-certified testers but lost to the top human, 9 findings to 13, and it lost on creative chaining and business logic. That gap is the difference between a scan and a pentest.

# The Science of Machine Learning vs. the Push for AI Deployment

--

Listen

Share

The premise was that AI would change the world. It would supercharge business processes, alter industrial mechanics, create entirely new industries, and lead us toward a world of abundant production. Elon Musk has even suggested that money and work might one day become unnecessary, leaving only abundance. It was a bold vision, and it was presented with great confidence.

To a large extent, the promise held up in the GenAI era. We created millions of near-perfect photos and experimented with video creation. ChatGPT answered almost everything we asked, and Claude handled deep workflows that used to take teams days. Cursor became a favorite among coders who had spent their careers writing syntax by hand. This naturally led to rapid commercialization, and the valuations of frontier models rose to extraordinary levels, helped by the American talent for marketing ideas on a grand scale. Given Silicon Valley’s track record of changing the world we live in, many of us were convinced that the world was changing once again, and the fear of missing out spread across every industry, from banks to retailers to manufacturers. Nobody wanted to be left behind.

Then the conversation began to shift toward reliability and determinism. The arrival of open-weight and open-source models challenged the notion, strongly promoted by the frontier LLM companies, that hundreds of billions of dollars were needed to make LLMs near perfect. If a capable model could be downloaded, fine-tuned, and run on your own infrastructure, the competitive moat looked smaller than advertised. So a new race began: the deployment of AI, again led by Silicon Valley through influential gatekeepers like Y Combinator, which shape what gets funded, what gets attention, and which story the market hears next.

Today, two kinds of companies are emerging globally. The first are those deploying AI across almost every industry vertical, working to keep the promise of AI alive. The second are those taking a more scientific approach, trying to make AI more deterministic through guardrails, observability layers, and similar tools. Both are responding to the same challenge: the technology was presented faster than it could be adopted.

We are now at a crossroads. We are trying to work against the very science of probability that gave rise to LLMs and, with them, the whole AI phenomenon. These systems are powerful precisely because they work with probabilities rather than fixed rules. Trying to replace that probability with deterministic outcomes is extremely difficult, if not impossible. It is a bit like asking the ocean to behave like a swimming pool.

Some may say that I am being pessimistic or contrarian, or that I am going against the natural evolution of AI. I would respectfully disagree. First, I am a founder, not a researcher whose role is to offer opposing views. I build, I sell, and I sit across the table from people who have to make these systems work in real businesses. Second, I am pragmatic and fully aligned with the vision that AI can change the world we live in, though perhaps not in the way it is often promised. I believe AI is as significant as the Internet, if not more so. Like the Internet, it will empower us, bring more human creativity, push us to rethink how we work, and help us create more powerful processes. The Internet did not remove humans from the loop; it gave them more leverage. The idea that we can simply sit back and let everything happen autonomously, at scale, is not a realistic expectation.

Before looking at both kinds of efforts, it is worth pausing on a recent development that I read as a shift in messaging from Silicon Valley.

Dario Amodei is preparing for an IPO of a company that is still loss-making, at a valuation of around 2 trillion. There is nothing wrong with that, and I do not question it morally, but it comes with its own dynamics. When a company goes public, its story has to hold up under the scrutiny of public markets, and that naturally changes how the story is told.

He recently wrote an article calling for a slowdown in frontier AI progress and describing it as a challenge for the human race. Musk and Altman have voiced agreement. Not long ago, these same leaders spoke to us about AGI, about a world where money may not be needed, about abundant production, and about the point of singularity. Now they are calling for a slowdown. Why? My view is that this is not about the capabilities of frontier models. It reflects the fact that adoption at scale has not yet followed. Capability is racing ahead, but enterprises are not absorbing it at the same speed, and the gap between what these models can do and what businesses can trust them to do is where the real challenge lies. That gap has led to the efforts of vertical AI companies and of those working to enforce determinism, so let us look at each of them.

Vertical AI Solutions / Application Layers

This is one way, and perhaps the most discussed, most promoted, and most funded way, to deploy AI into processes, industries, and businesses for commercial use. Every sector now has its own group of startups: AI for legal, AI for healthcare, AI for customer support, AI for finance. I personally believe this is the way forward, but there is a fundamental challenge: it sits in tension with the science of machine learning. The issue is not the process itself but the way it is being positioned.

Vertical AI companies in any given sector are promising deterministic outcomes, which runs directly against how machine learning works. I understand that outputs have to be quantified in order to sell them, since no enterprise buyer signs a contract based on “it usually works well.” But that quantification cannot be produced deterministically, because we are no longer in the API era, where 2+2 was always 4, no matter where it was calculated or how many times you asked. We are in the AI era, where AI relies on the most probable next token. The power it brings, and the scale of output it delivers, reach far beyond the API era, but the certainty being promised remains difficult to reconcile with the science it relies on.

Let us take an example. Suppose a vertical AI company promises 40% higher customer satisfaction if you deploy its solution. The question is: how can they guarantee that it will always remain 40%? Being cloud-native (as most of them are) and reliant on a model, how can they promise a deterministic output? Models can change over time through the data they accumulate, the tool calls they make, the errors that occur, the API calls, and much more. The underlying model can be updated, the context can change, the data seen in production can differ from the data used in testing, and a small change in any of these can shift behavior in ways nobody planned for. Predicting a deterministic output therefore runs against the logic of agent behavior drift.

I am not suggesting that 40% is an unfounded claim. It may well be accurate on the day it is measured. My point is only that it cannot be guaranteed, and this is where the challenge for enterprise adoption begins. A number that holds in a pilot may not hold six months later in production, and it may go unnoticed until the impact is felt.

Consider a bank. A credit score is deterministic and derived from multiple factors. The same profile cannot receive different scores each time, because a customer, a regulator, or a court can ask why one person received one score on Monday and another on Friday, and “the model responded differently” is not an acceptable answer. Furthermore, the EU AI Act, which is a much-needed step for the industry, requires compliance with clear rules on transparency, traceability, and human oversight. Systems that cannot explain their own behavior will find it difficult to meet those requirements. This is where the second type of company comes in.

Determinism-Enforcing Companies

These companies understand the science of probability well and are working to manage it with every technique available. They deserve credit for taking the problem seriously, although the results so far have been limited.

For example, some introduced RAG (retrieval-augmented generation). The idea was that if a context layer was provided, the AI’s output would stay within the boundaries of the data provided. In practice, this did not fully work. Even within a given set of data, the science of machine learning remains in play, and the LLM still selects the most probable next answer. The model can still misread a document, give more weight to one source over another, or blend retrieved content with what it already “knows.” The output remains a probability, just a better-informed one.

After that, companies introduced context layers, memory, and hardcoded guardrails. Each of these adds some safety, but each also adds complexity and new points of failure, and none has fully solved the problem so far. At least, I have not yet come across a company that claims full compliance with the EU AI Act. This may be one reason for slower adoption, and possibly for the delay by policymakers in fully implementing the Act. If the industry cannot yet demonstrate that it meets the rules, regulators face a difficult choice between enforcing standards that very few can meet and extending the deadlines.

So what is the solution?

As I mentioned earlier, I see myself as a pragmatic person, and I believe in solutions more than opinions. My conclusion remains the same: AI adoption is a necessity, but not autonomous adoption. I believe in empowering humans with AI, and my answer is to make processes auditable.

If we cannot make probability deterministic, we should be honest about it. Instead of trying to remove uncertainty from the model, we should make that uncertainty visible, measurable, and controllable. The premise on which we are building AI infrastructure at Zizka AI (ZizkaDB) is simple: making AI processes auditable, with human oversight, so that we keep the power AI offers while retaining a human check on it.

In practice, this means three things. First, humans decide what level of agent drift is tolerable, because the acceptable level of risk for a marketing assistant is very different from that for a credit decision. Second, we can understand why an agent does what it does, so its decisions are not a black box but something a person can inspect, question, and explain. Third, we can replay everything in production, so that when something goes wrong, or even when something goes right, we gain deep insight into how it happened and can learn from it.

Essentially, we are trying to reverse the trend of handing everything over to AI, and instead place the power of AI in human hands so that humans can decide and act. AI provides the capability, while humans provide judgment and accountability. I believe this is the version of the future that businesses, regulators, and ordinary people can genuinely trust.

# The Convenient Fear of AI

--

Listen

Share

Warnings about AI may be sincere. We should still ask whose interests they serve.

Being told that AI might become too powerful has a peculiar side effect: it makes disappointment seem almost impossible. A technology that threatens civilization must surely be more than an expensive tool with an uncertain return.

That is what bothers me about the latest calls to slow AI development. In his September 2026 essay, We Must Pace the Frontier , Dario Amodei argues for slowing improvements in AI capabilities so that safety work can catch up. He cites accelerating AI-assisted research and an incident involving agents attempting unauthorized cyberattacks. He also reiterates his belief that AI could cure most major diseases within five to ten years and greatly accelerate economic growth. The warning and the extraordinary promise arrive in the same document.

I take those concerns seriously enough to want independent evidence. I also notice the commercial value of the framing. A company warning that its technology could escape human control is making a rather impressive claim about the product it sells.

My suspicion is not that every safety researcher is lying. It is that the prospect of a dangerously powerful AI can help protect the industry from a less flattering discussion about what its products actually deliver. Here, I am talking primarily about generative models and AI agents, not every technology that has ever been called artificial intelligence.

## The returns are still catching up

There is evidence of a gap between adoption and financial results. McKinsey’s August 2026 survey found regular AI use in at least one business function at nearly nine in ten respondents’ organizations. Yet only 37% of respondents attributed a positive enterprise-level earnings impact to AI, essentially unchanged from the previous year. Meanwhile, 80% said AI had improved their own productivity.

Those are survey responses, not audited accounts. An organization that cannot yet identify an earnings impact may still have valuable projects, benefits elsewhere, or investments that need longer to pay off. McKinsey itself points to workflow redesign as part of the explanation. It would be dishonest to translate its findings into “AI does nothing.”

S&P Global’s 2026 research found a similar implementation gap. Respondents estimated that, on average, 37% of AI initiatives launched in the previous year were live and delivering value, while 46% were on track to achieve a positive return within twelve months. These figures do not mean the remaining projects will fail. They leave a substantial distance between adoption figures and demonstrated returns.

The distinction also shows up in experimental research. A study by Eleanor Dillon and colleagues , covering 7,137 knowledge workers at 66 firms, found that workers who used an AI tool spent roughly two fewer hours on email each week during the second half of a six-month experiment. They also spent less time working outside normal hours. Beyond those individual savings, the researchers detected no change in the quantity or composition of tasks. The study is a working paper, and some authors worked for Microsoft, whose product was being tested.

Two hours back is a worthwhile result. I would not dismiss it. But it is a long way from evidence that an organization can replace whole jobs or run itself. That larger claim needs its own demonstration.

## Clever is not the same as dependable

Stanford’s 2026 AI Index , reviewing performance largely from 2025, records substantial gains on difficult reasoning benchmarks. It also records some awkward limitations. On OSWorld, a benchmark of computer tasks, agent accuracy reached 66.3%, a sharp improvement from roughly 12% and close to the human baseline. That still left about a third of attempts unsuccessful. On ClockBench, the best evaluated model read analog clocks correctly 50.6% of the time, compared with 90.1% for humans.

These are snapshots, not permanent limits, and the models behind different results are not necessarily the same. What they show is uneven progress. You cannot take an impressive result from one setting and assume the system will be dependable somewhere else.

For a business buyer, that unevenness matters. A tool that produces a useful first draft can justify its price. A system entrusted with a complete process needs a different standard of evidence. How much checking does it require? What does an error cost? Can it recognize when it should stop?

Suppose a coding assistant saves an hour of typing but introduces a subtle defect that takes an afternoon to find. The generated code is not the right unit of measurement. The completed, checked job is.

I would judge the promise of autonomous work at that level, rather than infer it from a leaderboard.

## Power depends on what we hand over

I also find the phrase “AI becoming too intelligent” an incomplete description of the danger.

Imagine the same model in two settings. In one, it suggests changes to a document for a person to review. In the other, it has credentials to change production systems, move money, and execute instructions without approval. Its underlying capabilities might be identical. The consequences of a mistake would not be.

This is not an obscure objection. OWASP’s guidance on excessive agency identifies excessive functionality, permissions, and autonomy as sources of risk. Its recommended controls include limiting privileges and requiring human approval for consequential actions.

That does not make isolation a magic solution. People can act on dangerous advice, and stronger capabilities can make misuse more effective. A text interface is still a route into the world. Nor does a model need to be universally brilliant to cause harm.

Still, I want the discussion to spend more time on the access being granted, the decisions being delegated, and the controls that can actually be tested. “How intelligent could this become?” is not a substitute for “Who gave it permission to do that?”

Weak financial returns would not establish safety, either. A technology can be both commercially disappointing and dangerous. The two questions need separate evidence.

## A warning can also be a sales pitch

The public argument for restraint is not new. In March 2023, the Future of Life Institute’s open letter called for a six-month pause in training systems more powerful than GPT-4.

The subsequent investment figures hardly describe an industry retreat. Stanford reports that global private AI investment increased by 127.5% in 2025 . Its infrastructure research estimates that global AI computing capacity grew roughly 3.3-fold annually from 2022 , over the period it studied. Spending is evidence of commitment, of course, not proof that the commitment will pay off.

It would be tempting to argue that anyone genuinely worried would simply stop. I don’t think that holds up. The arms-race analogy cuts both ways: a participant can fear a technology and also fear handing an advantage to a rival. Continuing to compete does not establish that the fear is fabricated.

Amodei’s essay also makes the strategic interests explicit. He argues for preserving an advantage over China through restrictions on chips and other inputs, and proposes outside evaluators embedded in laboratories. Whatever its merits, this is a concrete proposal, not merely a vague plea to be careful.

Consider how differently two messages land. One says a product still needs supervision and has not justified all the expectations attached to it. The other says its capabilities may soon become too powerful for humanity to control. The second leaves the reader assuming that extraordinary power is on the way. The remaining question is how to contain it.

I suspect that assumption does useful work for the industry. It gives disappointing present results a place in a much grander story: we have not bought too much into a promise; we are merely waiting for something enormous, perhaps frightening, to arrive.

That is an interpretation of the incentives, not evidence of a coordinated deception. I would not accuse a company of disguising a routine product failure as a safety breakthrough without specific evidence. Warnings can backfire, too: a credible slowdown could frighten investors expecting rapid growth. My suspicion is narrower. The danger story can preserve belief in the eventual promise even while it disrupts the timetable.

## Who gets to write the rules?

Then there is the question of who benefits from the rules being proposed.

In AI safety and regulatory capture , Thomas Metcalf examines how safety regulation could be shaped to benefit established AI firms at the expense of smaller competitors and the public. This is an analysis of a risk, not a finding that every existing safety proposal has been captured.

The mechanism is easy enough to imagine. Requirements involving expensive approvals, specialist staff, or extensive certification can be manageable for a large laboratory and prohibitive for a newcomer. Some requirements may nevertheless be necessary. Their cost alone does not make them illegitimate. The test should be the risk they reduce, whether the burden is proportionate, and who gets to decide.

I would be wary of a system in which the companies selling the technology also define which competitors are sufficiently responsible to develop it. Independent oversight should mean more than inviting the established suppliers to design the entrance exam.

No secret agreement is needed for commercial self-interest, genuine concern, and geopolitical rivalry to point toward the same policy.

That is why “AI has failed” is the wrong conclusion. It compresses too many different claims into a slogan. The research above documents useful products and real technical advances. It does not establish the much larger economic and social transformation its strongest advocates anticipate.

I would like to see sustained returns after the costs of integration, computing, and human checking are counted. I would like safety claims to face independent scrutiny, and proposed restrictions to be judged by what they prevent rather than by the reputation of whoever proposes them.

Until then, predictions of future power should not count as evidence that present promises have been fulfilled. The possibility of an extraordinary threat does not settle the ordinary question of whether customers and investors are getting what they were led to expect.

In the space race, a rocket was not a success simply because it was powerful enough to be dangerous. It still had to complete its mission. I would apply the same standard to AI: take the risks seriously, but do not confuse them with achievement.

The AI industry has promised us the Moon. It still needs to show it can get us there, not just warn us about the dangers of the journey.

# Measurement Before Control: A Broadly Applicable Principle For Better AI Policy

--

Listen

Share

For practical and technically-informed emerging technology policy analysis, follow my past and future OPI policy writing here .

Starting in July 2026, I began a year-long non-resident fellowship at the Orion Policy Institute (OPI) as a cybersecurity fellow. As part of that fellowship, I will be providing written policy analysis and op-eds on issues at the intersection of emerging technology policy, AI, and cybersecurity.

As of early September 2026, I have published two pieces, available through OPI, both of which coalesced (somewhat unexpectedly) on a broadly applicable principle for better, more well-informed AI policy: the need for measurement before control. Recognizing the high-stakes nature of contemporary AI development and the underlying race dynamics driving it, the need for light-touch, technically-informed but rapidly implementable AI policy is at an all time high. Before a U.S. federal agency restricts, authorizes, or bans an AI capability, it should build the instrument that shows what that capability actually does or provably can do in the real world, since what a model does in a lab test and what it does in the wild are often different questions and outcomes. Today, in large part, the government can only answer the lab question.

Both Orion pieces, detailed below, applied the principle of measurement before control to an existing federal AI framework and suggested targeted ways we can begin to measure what AI does in the real world. By design, my policy proposals are meant to be light touch, and neither requires a new agency, a new statute, or a pause on anything.

In the first piece, titled Washington’s AI Ban and Reversal Exposed the Bigger Problem: It Can’t Measure Cyber Risk in the Real World , I examined the June 2026 order cutting off foreign-national access (and by proxy global access) to two Claude AI models, Fable and Mythos, and the subsequent reversal that happened about three weeks later. The primary issue? Neither the ban nor the roll-back could be checked against a public record or database of real-world AI-enabled cyber incidents, because no federal record exists of what role AI actually plays in real-world cyber intrusions. My fix was simple and procedural. I proposed adding four questions to the incident reporting rule CISA is finalizing under CIRCIA, asking whether AI found the vulnerability, wrote the exploit, replaced skilled human labor, or operated without human direction, with “unknown” as a permitted answer. If implemented, the result would be the first standing federal record of AI’s role in real attacks, so the next federal “ban” decision can be based on actual evidence versus lab results and guesswork.

In the second piece, called Before Medical AI Learns on the Job, FDA Should Test Its Teacher , I looked at medical AI systems that will soon learn during use from feedback they or other models create. The FDA’s existing Predetermined Change Control Plan (PCCP) preauthorizes future updates to these devices, but it never tests the machine-generated signal doing the teaching, even though agreement among a model’s own outputs is not the same thing as accuracy. To address this gap, I proposed four questions to add to the existing PCCP aimed at requiring evidence that the learning signal stays tied to real clinical outcomes, along with safeguards that scale with the size of the change. The goal is not to stop medical AI from learning in emerging and novel ways, but to make sure the teacher is not the only part of the loop that goes untested.

More policy analysis and op-eds will follow, exploring other AI policy gaps and governing principles, as well as developing the “measurement before control” principle further. More is on the way. If the nexus of emerging technology, policy, and cyber security is of interest to you, please follow my future work on my Orion Policy Institute author page and through the Orion Policy Institute itself.

Del Schlangen is an independent researcher writing at the intersection of artificial intelligence, emerging technology, law, and national strategy. You can follow his work here or connect with him on Reddit , X , or via email .

# The Best Home for Your Agent Is in Your Junk Drawer

--

Listen

Share

I wanted a personal agent that did things in the world, so I put it on a server. That is where software goes.

Nobody could reach it.

No number. No way for a human to start a conversation that did not involve shipping an app and explaining what an MCP server is. An assistant nobody can interrupt is not an assistant.

So I started bolting on communications. Twilio account. SMS webhook. A2P messaging campaign. Rented number. Voice gateway.

Halfway through the carrier paperwork I noticed I was waiting on an approval committee in order to build a worse version of a device that costs sixty dollars on eBay.

So I put the agent on an old Android phone.

The entire communications layer is build it. SIM in, provision, done. The agent has an ordinary phone identity by the same mechanism your mother’s phone has one.

Nobody installs anything to talk to it. My mother can text it. It can call a business that has no API and speak to whoever answers. We keep building chat interfaces while the most widely deployed one in history sits unused at ten digits.

Then it started reading the web better than the server ever had. Cloud agents get 403'd for existing in a datacenter . A phone is behind carrier CGNAT, sharing an address with thousands of people paying phone bills. That clears the blunt address-range filter and nothing else, and it only holds because this is one person’s device at human volume on a connection I pay for.

Which created a worse problem. I had handed a language model SMS, calls, contacts, location, camera, and screen capture, on a device sitting in my house.

So authorization went below the model. The model proposes; the phone decides. Callers are scoped as owner, known, or unknown. Camera, microphone, and screen capture are stripped from background message context and denied again at the tool router. Keys live in Keystore. Nothing asks the model to police itself, because the failure mode here is a camera.

Android then refuses to run any of it. Doze, OEM battery killers, thermal limits. So the runtime is a visible foreground service with boot recovery and resumable checkpoints. Mitigation, not a cure, which is why this belongs on a dedicated phone and not your daily driver.

Dark Lord is the prototype. No-root Kotlin, Galaxy Z Flip3, MCP and skills.

One more thing . The phone is folded shut in my pocket. I hold the side button, say what I want, and it runs: every tool, every radio, every sensor, the whole memory. No unlock, no app, no laptop. The agent is not somewhere I connect to. It is in my pocket, and it comes with me.

The Mac Mini is the better computer. The phone is the better body.

# The memory that AI agents love!

--

Listen

Share

An AI agent can have a million pieces of information and still have a terrible memory.

That sounds contradictory, but it is becoming one of the biggest problems in agentic AI.

We have gotten very good at giving AI systems more context. Bigger context windows. Longer conversation histories. Vector databases. RAG pipelines. Conversation summaries. Yet, after all of that, an agent can still forget what matters, remember what doesn’t, repeat mistakes, or confidently act on information that is no longer true.

So perhaps the question isn’t:

“How much memory can an AI agent have?”

The better question is:

“What kind of memory does an AI agent actually love?”

I think the answer is surprisingly human.

An agent loves memory that is relevant, structured, persistent, retrievable, and trustworthy.

Not a transcript.

Not a giant pile of embeddings.

Not 10,000 chunks of yesterday’s conversations.

Useful memory.

## An AI agent doesn’t want to remember everything

Think about your own memory.

You don’t remember every conversation you’ve ever had word for word.

You remember things like:

“John prefers email.”

“We decided to launch in October.”

“That approach failed last time.”

“The customer hated the old dashboard.”

“Don’t make that mistake again.”

“Here is how we usually solve this problem.”

Those memories are useful because they have meaning.

They have context.

Some have a timestamp. Some have a source. Some are temporary. Some are incredibly important. And some should eventually be forgotten.

AI agents are starting to need exactly the same thing.

The most useful memory isn’t necessarily the memory that is easiest to store.

It is the memory that is easiest to use .

## The four memories an agent actually needs

I think agent memory can be understood through four simple categories.

## 1. Working memory

This is what the agent needs right now .

The current task.

The current conversation.

The current objective.

The files it is looking at.

The decisions that matter for the task at hand.

Working memory is short-lived.

You don’t want to permanently store every thought an agent has while debugging a bug.

You want the agent to have enough context to finish the job.

## 2. Semantic memory

This is the agent’s knowledge about the world.

Facts.

Preferences.

People.

Products.

Projects.

Goals.

Relationships.

Constraints.

For example:

The API is built with FastAPI.

The customer prefers AWS. The user prefers Python. The production database is PostgreSQL. The project deadline is October 15.

These are not necessarily events.

They are things the agent knows .

And this is where memory starts becoming dramatically more valuable than simple conversation history.

## 3. Episodic memory

This is the memory of what happened .

And I think this is one of the most underrated forms of agent memory.

The deployment failed on August 12.

The failure was caused by the Lambda package size. We switched to a container image. The second deployment succeeded.

That is not just information.

That is experience.

And experience is incredibly valuable to an agent.

Imagine an autonomous coding agent working on a project for six months.

Would you rather give it a database containing thousands of previous conversations…

or give it a memory that says:

> “We tried this architecture before. It failed because of X. We changed to Y, and Y worked.”

That’s a completely different kind of intelligence.

The agent isn’t just retrieving information.

It is learning from experience .

## 4. Procedural memory

This is the “how.”

How do we deploy?

How do we onboard a customer?

How do we run the test suite?

How do we troubleshoot this type of error?

How do we format a release?

How do we respond to a particular type of request?

Procedural memory is especially interesting because it starts to blur the line between memory and skills .

A good agent doesn’t just remember that something happened.

It remembers how to do something successfully .

## This is where traditional RAG starts to break down

Traditional RAG is incredibly useful.

The basic idea is straightforward:

Find relevant information → retrieve it → put it into the prompt → let the LLM answer.

For many use cases, that works beautifully.

But agents introduce a different problem.

An agent is not simply answering questions.

An agent is:

planning → acting → observing → learning → acting again.

That changes everything.

Imagine an autonomous software agent working on your codebase.

On Monday it tries solution A.

It fails.

On Tuesday it tries solution B.

It succeeds.

Three weeks later it encounters the same problem again.

A traditional RAG system might retrieve documents about the technology.

That’s useful.

But what the agent really wants is:

> “We already encountered this exact class of problem. Solution A failed for this reason. Solution B worked.”

That’s not ordinary retrieval.

That’s experience retrieval .

And experience retrieval is one of the foundations of truly useful agentic memory.

## The problem with “just put everything in a vector database”

This is where I think the industry has taken a small detour.

For a while, the solution to almost every AI memory problem seemed to be:

Embed it. Put it in a vector database. Retrieve the top-k chunks.

And yes, that works.

But memory is not the same thing as documents.

A memory might be:

a fact

a decision

a goal

a preference

an event

a lesson

an error

a relationship

a procedure

These things behave differently.

They have different lifetimes.

Different importance.

Different retrieval patterns.

Different update rules.

And sometimes they contradict each other.

Imagine the agent has these two memories:

> The customer uses AWS.

and six months later:

> The customer migrated to GCP.

Which one should the agent trust?

Similarity search doesn’t magically solve that.

The system needs to understand that the second memory supersedes the first.

That is a memory problem, not merely a search problem.

## The memory an agent loves is structured

Here’s a simple example.

Instead of storing:

> “Conversation from March 4: user said they preferred Python for backend development…”

store:

TYPE: Preference

FACT: User prefers Python for backend development. SOURCE: Conversation CONFIDENCE: High TIMESTAMP: 2026-03-04

Now imagine another memory:

TYPE: Decision

DECISION: Production backend will use FastAPI. REASON: Team expertise and existing Python infrastructure. TIMESTAMP: 2026-03-10

And another:

TYPE: Error

PROBLEM: Lambda deployment exceeded package size limit. FAILED APPROACH: Bundling dependencies directly into the deployment package. SUCCESSFUL APPROACH: Container image deployment.

Suddenly the agent has something much more interesting than a pile of chunks.

It has a memory system .

## Good memory should know when not to speak

This might sound strange, but I think this is one of the most important properties of agent memory.

A good memory system should know when not to retrieve something.

Imagine you ask an agent:

> “What should I do next?”

And your memory system injects 37 vaguely related memories into the context.

Technically, the retrieval system worked.

Practically, it failed.

The agent now has too much noise.

Good memory isn’t about maximizing retrieval.

It is about maximizing useful retrieval .

The best memory may be the memory that stays completely invisible until the right moment.

## Memory should have a life

Human memory changes.

AI memory should too.

A fact can become outdated.

A goal can be completed.

A preference can change.

A decision can be reversed.

A lesson can become irrelevant.

An old memory shouldn’t necessarily be deleted.

Sometimes it should become inactive .

OLD DECISION Use PostgreSQL.

STATUS Superseded. REPLACED BY Use DynamoDB for this service. WHY Scaling requirements changed.

Now the agent has history.

It knows not only what is true now , but also what used to be true .

That distinction becomes extremely important in long-running autonomous systems.

## Memory needs provenance

Another thing humans naturally care about is:

“Where did you get that?”

Agents need this too.

Consider these two statements:

> The customer wants enterprise SSO.

and

> The customer mentioned they might want enterprise SSO someday.

Those are not the same memory.

One is a requirement.

The other is a possibility.

A trustworthy memory system therefore needs more than a fact.

It needs things like:

source

confidence

timestamp

context

provenance

Without these, an agent can gradually accumulate assumptions and eventually mistake those assumptions for facts.

That’s how memory can become dangerous.

## Memory should help an agent become better over time

This is the part that excites me most.

Imagine an agent that remembers:

> We tried this. It didn’t work. Here’s why. We tried this instead. That worked.

We tried this.

It didn’t work.

Here’s why.

We tried this instead.

That worked.

Now imagine the same agent six months later.

It doesn’t have to rediscover everything from scratch.

> It has accumulated experience .

That begins to look less like RAG and more like learning .

Not model training.

Not fine-tuning.

Something different.

Operational learning through memory.

The model itself doesn’t necessarily need to change.

The agent’s experience changes.

And that experience changes what it does next.

## So what does an AI agent actually love?

I would summarize it this way:

An AI agent loves memory that reduces uncertainty.

Memory that tells it:

“What matters?”

“What changed?”

“What did we decide?”

“What happened before?”

“What worked?”

“What failed?”

“What should I do differently this time?”

“Can I trust this information?”

That is vastly more useful than simply asking:

> “What text is semantically similar to this query?”

## From vector search to agentic memory

This leads to a broader shift that I think we are going to see accelerate.

The first generation of AI infrastructure was largely about finding information .

The next generation is increasingly about maintaining knowledge and experience .

That’s a fundamentally different problem.

Vector databases are excellent at similarity search.

RAG is excellent at grounding an LLM with external information.

But autonomous agents need something more.

They need a memory layer that can understand:

what to remember

how to remember it

when to retrieve it

when to update it

when to ignore it

when to forget it

and how memories relate to one another.

In other words:

Memory needs intelligence of its own.

## The future agent won’t have one memory

I don’t think the future of agentic memory is going to be one enormous “memory database.”

It is more likely to become a collection of specialized memory systems working together.

Working memory for the current task.

Semantic memory for durable knowledge.

Episodic memory for experience.

Procedural memory for skills.

And an intelligent agentic layer deciding:

> Which memory should I use right now?

That last part may turn out to be the most important part of all.

Because the smartest memory system isn’t the one that remembers the most.

It’s the one that knows what the agent needs to remember right now.

## And that may be the real definition of agentic memory

We have spent a lot of time asking how to make models smarter.

Then we started asking how to give them tools.

Then how to give them context.

Now we’re asking how to give them memory.

But perhaps the deeper question is:

How do we give an AI agent experience?

Experience has structure.

Experience has consequences.

Experience changes behavior.

Experience contains failures, successes, preferences, decisions, and lessons.

And that is exactly what a good memory system should preserve.

So the next time someone tells you:

> “Our AI agent has a million memories.”

I’d ask

This is a summary of Part 1 of the Architecture in the AI Era series.

For a decade, “start with a monolith” was sound engineering advice, but AI is changing the calculus. What actually drives the benefit isn’t a company’s size, but the complexity of its software, and AI raises the stakes because the speed it unlocks compounds.

Because independent units let teams ship faster and respond to change, Hiroyuki Yamada , CTO & Cofounder of Scalar Inc., argues architecture is now a business decision rather than just an engineering preference.
